title: Level 3 Final Assessment
quiz.0.question: Timorasso is a rare white grape of which Italian region, and which producer has brought it renewed international attention?
quiz.0.options.1: The Colli Tortonesi in Piemonte, revived by Walter Massa
quiz.0.options.3: Tuscany, revived by the Antinori family
quiz.0.explanation: Timorasso is an old white grape of the Colli Tortonesi in eastern Piemonte that came close to extinction; Walter Massa has worked to revive it since the 1980s. Its wines are known for high acidity, minerality and long ageing potential, and it has been called "Italy's Riesling".
quiz.1.question: Ruché (or Ruchè) is a rare red grape of which Italian region, and what aromatic character is it known for?
quiz.1.options.0: Veneto, known for black fruit and chocolate
quiz.1.options.1: Castagnole Monferrato in Piemonte, known for perfumed rose petal and spice
quiz.1.explanation: Ruché (Ruchè) is a native red grape of the Monferrato hills in Piemonte, awarded DOCG status in 2010 (Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato DOCG). It is famous for its distinctive rose-petal, violet and spice aromas, in a style between the elegance of Pinot Noir and the perfume of Gewürztraminer.
quiz.2.question: Where is Erbaluce di Caluso DOCG, and what special wine is it known for?
quiz.2.options.1: The Canavese in Piemonte, known for Caluso Passito (a sweet white from dried grapes) and dry whites
quiz.2.options.2: Trentino-Alto Adige, known for sparkling wine
quiz.2.options.3: Umbria, known for high-acid sweet whites
quiz.2.explanation: Erbaluce di Caluso DOCG lies in the Canavese hills of Piemonte, north of Turin. Caluso Passito, made from dried Erbaluce grapes, is a golden sweet white and one of Piemonte's most precious sweet wines, while the dry version is known for high acidity and minerality.
quiz.3.question: Where does Vino Santo, the most important wine made from the Nosiola grape, come from?
quiz.3.options.1: The Valle dei Laghi (valley of the lakes) in Trentino
quiz.3.explanation: Nosiola is Trentino's most important native white grape, at its best in the Valle dei Laghi (at the northern end of Lake Garda). Vino Santo Trentino made from Nosiola uses appassimento: the grapes are dried until Holy Week of the following year (about 5-6 months) before pressing, then aged for many years in wood — one of Italy's rarest sweet whites.
quiz.4.question: Who is the most important pioneer of the modern revival of orange wine (skin-contact white wine), and where?
quiz.4.options.1: Josko Gravner, Oslavia in Friuli, late 1990s
quiz.4.explanation: Josko Gravner is the pioneer of the modern orange-wine movement: in the late 1990s, in Oslavia in Friuli, he began macerating white grapes on their skins for long periods (6+ months) in clay vessels (qvevri/amphora), reviving an ancient Georgian tradition and sparking a global orange-wine revolution.
quiz.5.question: What is the core winemaking principle of orange wine (skin-contact white)?
quiz.5.options.0: Blending red grapes into white juice to extract a pink colour
quiz.5.options.1: Fermenting white grapes on their skins (maceration), extracting tannin, polyphenols and an orange-amber colour
quiz.5.options.2: Ageing white wine in old Port casks to give it an orange colour
quiz.5.options.3: Adding natural food colouring after winemaking
quiz.5.explanation: The core of orange wine is fermenting white grapes in contact with their skins (and seeds), extracting tannins, phenolic pigments and polyphenols that give an orange to amber colour, along with red-wine-like structure and oxidative complexity — the most controversial and most watched new style among whites.
quiz.6.question: In the Barolo DOCG MGA system, what different terroirs do Vigna Rionda in Serralunga d'Alba and Brunate in La Morra represent?
quiz.6.options.0: The two have the same soil; only the place name differs
quiz.6.options.1: Serralunga (Serravallian strata, formerly called Helvetian): calcareous marl and sandstone, poor and compact, firm tannins needing long ageing; La Morra (Tortonian strata): looser calcareous marl, aromatic and elegant, opening earlier
quiz.6.options.2: Vigna Rionda is on flat land and Brunate on a hilltop; altitude is the only difference
quiz.6.options.3: La Morra may only produce Riserva, Serralunga only normal Barolo
quiz.6.explanation: Barolo's most important geological divide: Serralunga d'Alba (Serravallian strata, formerly Helvetian; calcareous marl and sandstone, poor and compact) → a powerful frame and tight tannins needing 15-25 years of ageing; La Morra and Barolo village (Tortonian strata, looser calcareous marl) → aromatic, supple and relatively early to open. This is the core geological meaning behind the terroir differences of the MGAs.
quiz.7.question: What is the main function of the Italian DOCG neck seal (fascetta)?
quiz.7.options.1: A uniquely numbered seal issued under state control, preventing counterfeit DOCG wine and recording the production lot
quiz.7.options.2: Showing the wine's best drinking year
quiz.7.options.3: Proof that import/export duties have been paid
quiz.7.explanation: The fascetta (state guarantee seal) is the core identification tool of Italian DOCG: every bottle has a unique serial number, printed by the State Printing Office (Poligrafico dello Stato) and issued through authorised certification bodies; it spans the closure, making it hard to forge or reuse — the most reliable external mark for consumers to verify a genuine DOCG.
quiz.8.question: What is the legal meaning of "Riserva" on an Italian label?
quiz.8.options.0: Made only in the best years, with quality decided subjectively by the winemaker
quiz.8.options.1: Meets a longer minimum ageing requirement than the normal wine (oak + bottle), with rules varying by DOC/DOCG
quiz.8.options.2: Made only from the oldest vines (60+ years) of selected vineyards
quiz.8.options.3: A uniform rule for every DOCG: at least 5 years before release
quiz.8.explanation: "Riserva" has clear minimum ageing requirements in Italian law, but they vary by DOC/DOCG: Barolo Riserva needs 62 months, Barbaresco Riserva 50 months, Brunello di Montalcino Riserva over 6 years. What they share is that a Riserva must be aged longer than the normal wine.
quiz.9.question: In assessing Italian vintages, which climate factor has the greatest influence on late-ripening grapes (such as Nebbiolo and Aglianico)?
quiz.9.options.2: Autumn rain before harvest in September-October (diluting sugar and causing rot)
quiz.9.options.3: Spring frost in April-May (affecting fruit set)
quiz.9.explanation: Nebbiolo and Aglianico are very late-ripening grapes, usually harvested from mid-October into November. Autumn rain is the greatest risk: persistent rain in September-October dilutes the juice (lowering sugar and polyphenol concentration) and triggers grey rot (Botrytis) — the most decisive climate factor for a good or bad vintage for these grapes.
quiz.10.question: Among Barolo's most famous top vintages (close to "five stars"), which are most recognised by collectors?
quiz.10.explanation: 2010 and 2016 are recognised as Barolo's greatest recent vintages: both deliver perfect Nebbiolo ripeness with fresh acidity and precise structure, with ageing potential of 30-50+ years, and are seen by many critics and collectors as outstanding vintages.
quiz.11.question: What is the special significance of the 1997 vintage of Brunello di Montalcino?
quiz.11.options.0: The first vintage in Italian wine history to score 100 points
quiz.11.options.1: A hot, dry year gave rich, ripe fruit; it was officially rated five stars and enthusiastically praised by international critics, greatly raising Brunello's international profile
quiz.11.options.2: The first time the government allowed 15% other grapes in Brunello
quiz.11.options.3: Severe rot meant almost every estate decided not to make Brunello
quiz.11.explanation: 1997 was hot and dry, giving Brunello lush, ripe fruit; the producers' consortium (Consorzio) rated it a five-star vintage and international critics praised it enthusiastically, sending Brunello's fame and prices soaring — an important milestone in Brunello's move into the international collectors' market. Over time, however, some wines were judged to have matured quickly, and more balanced vintages have aged longer.
quiz.12.question: What are the ideal storage conditions for a wine cellar?
quiz.12.options.0: 18-22°C, 50-60% humidity, strong light to speed up maturation
quiz.12.options.1: 12-14°C, 70-75% humidity, no temperature swings, dark, no strong vibration
quiz.12.options.3: The colder the better (0-4°C), fully sealed with no need for humidity control
quiz.12.explanation: Ideal cellar conditions: 12-14°C (stability matters most — big swings are more harmful than a slightly high temperature), 70-75% humidity (preventing corks from drying and cracking, though too high encourages mould), complete darkness (UV damages phenolic compounds), no vibration (which disturbs tartrate deposits), bottles lying down (keeping the cork moist).
quiz.13.question: Why should wine usually be stored lying down?
quiz.13.options.0: To save space and make cellar management easier
quiz.13.options.1: To keep the cork in contact with the wine, preventing it from drying and shrinking, which would let air in
quiz.13.options.2: To make remuage easier and gather the sediment
quiz.13.options.3: Only sparkling wine needs to lie down; still wine doesn't matter
quiz.13.explanation: Storing bottles on their side keeps the inside of the cork moist, preventing shrinkage and micro-oxidation caused by drying. A dry cork loses its seal and speeds up oxidative ageing. Wines under screwcap (Stelvin) need not lie down; storing them upright does not affect quality.
quiz.14.question: What is the correct systematic order of the SAT blind-tasting method (Sight / Aroma / Taste)?
quiz.14.options.0: Taste first, then look at the colour, and smell last
quiz.14.options.1: First observe the appearance (colour, clarity, viscosity) → smell the aromas (once still, then swirled) → taste (attack, mid-palate, finish, aftertaste)
quiz.14.options.2: Smell first, then taste, and look at the colour last
quiz.14.options.3: SAT has no fixed order; it depends on personal habit
quiz.14.explanation: The standard SAT order: S (sight) → A (aroma) → T (taste). Appearance assesses depth of colour, hue, viscosity (legs) and clarity; aroma is assessed still then swirled, distinguishing primary (varietal), secondary (fermentation) and tertiary (ageing) aromas; taste assesses acidity, sweetness, tannin and alcohol, before concluding (grape, area, vintage).
quiz.15.question: In blind tasting, what is the most typical combination of features for identifying Nebbiolo?
quiz.15.options.0: Deep purple, blackcurrant + tobacco, high alcohol
quiz.15.options.1: Pale garnet + orange-red rim, tar + rose + dried leaves, high acid and high tannin
quiz.15.options.2: Deep ruby, blackberry + mint, medium acidity
quiz.15.options.3: Pale gold, pear blossom + stone, low tannin (a white)
quiz.15.explanation: Nebbiolo's three identifiers: 1) sight: pale garnet with an orange rim (even when young); 2) aroma: tar + rose + dried leaves are the classic Barolo/Barbaresco aromas; 3) palate: very high acidity + very high tannin, one of the most extreme combinations among Italian red grapes.
quiz.16.question: In blind tasting, how do you tell Sangiovese (Chianti Classico) from Barbera d'Asti?
quiz.16.options.0: They cannot be told apart; you must check the label
quiz.16.options.1: Sangiovese: high acid + medium tannin + herbal, tomato-leaf notes; Barbera: even higher acidity + lower tannin + pure, bright red fruit
quiz.16.options.2: Barbera is always paler than Sangiovese
quiz.16.options.3: Sangiovese is always at least 2% higher in alcohol than Barbera
quiz.16.explanation: The key difference: Barbera has very low tannin (sometimes barely noticeable) but acidity that can be even higher than Sangiovese's, with pure, tangy red fruit (sour cherry, raspberry); Sangiovese has noticeable tannin and Chianti's tomato-leaf, dried-herb and leather notes. Tannin is the quickest point of distinction on the palate.
quiz.17.question: In blind tasting, how do you tell a high-quality Alto Adige Pinot Grigio from an industrial Veneto version?
quiz.17.options.0: They cannot be told apart; they are identical
quiz.17.options.1: Alto Adige: more concentrated, with minerality, almond, ripe fruit and fresh acidity; the industrial Veneto version: thin and neutral, watery, lacking character
quiz.17.options.2: The Alto Adige version is always sweet, the Veneto version always dry
quiz.17.options.3: The industrial version always exceeds 14% alcohol, the quality version is always under 12%
quiz.17.explanation: Alto Adige Pinot Grigio, grown at altitude with wide day-night temperature swings, keeps more natural acidity and concentration, with minerality, almond and ripe fruit. The industrial Veneto version, under pressure for high yields, is thin in flavour — the root of Pinot Grigio's poor reputation. (Separately, the traditional Ramato style of Friuli and the Veneto uses brief skin contact to give a coppery-pink colour.)
quiz.18.question: What is preparation 500, the core preparation of Italian biodynamics (biodinamica)?
quiz.18.options.0: A special fertiliser spray containing 500 minerals
quiz.18.options.1: Cow manure packed into a cow horn and buried in the soil, fermented over winter, then dug up, diluted, stirred and sprayed on the land
quiz.18.options.2: Using exactly 500 litres of organic compost per hectare
quiz.18.options.3: An organic liquid fertiliser applied every May (the 5th month)
quiz.18.explanation: Preparation 500 (horn manure) is the core of Rudolf Steiner's biodynamics: cow manure is packed into cow horns and buried in the soil over winter (about 6 months) to ferment; once dug up, a small amount is dissolved in water and stirred dynamically for about 1 hour to form an "activated" preparation, then sprayed on the vineyard soil to enliven its microbial life.
quiz.19.question: What is the short-term effect of climate warming on high-altitude vineyards in northern Italy (such as Alto Adige and Valtellina)?
quiz.19.options.0: An immediate fall in grape quality, hitting high altitudes hardest
quiz.19.options.1: Possibly beneficial in the short term: warmer temperatures let late-ripening grapes ripen more reliably and raise the upper altitude limit for planting
quiz.19.options.2: No effect at all; the mountain climate is insulated from global warming
quiz.19.options.3: It affects only irrigation needs, not quality
quiz.19.explanation: In the short term (a 10-30-year view), warming has some positive effects for high-altitude northern Italy: more reliable ripeness (especially for late-ripening grapes) and a higher altitude limit for planting, making once-too-cold sites suitable for vines. In the long term (50+ years), more extreme summer heat, water stress and the need to change grape varieties are the core threats.
quiz.20.question: What are the long-term challenges of climate warming for viticulture in southern Italy (Sicily, Puglia)?
quiz.20.options.0: The South will benefit from warming, with greatly improved grape quality
quiz.20.options.1: Continued warming worsens water shortages, raises alcohol and causes loss of acidity, affecting the quality of top wines
quiz.20.options.2: Warming lets the South start growing Nebbiolo, which was impossible before
quiz.20.options.3: Almost no effect — the South is already hot and adapted to heat
quiz.20.explanation: The long-term risks of warming in the South: scarcer water (Puglia already faces severe drought), alcohol increasingly hard to keep in a reasonable range, and continued loss of natural acidity (affecting balance and ageing potential); traditional low-altitude areas may face difficulty growing vines in future, and moving to higher altitudes is the main response.
quiz.21.question: What is the most controversial winemaking principle of Italian natural wine (vino naturale)?
quiz.21.options.0: No pesticides at all, fully organic farming
quiz.21.options.1: Adding no or very little sulphur dioxide (SO₂) during winemaking, accepting the wine's natural evolution and instability
quiz.21.options.3: Winemaking must take place in amphorae
quiz.21.explanation: The core controversy of natural wine is the use of sulphur dioxide: natural producers advocate adding none or very little (only a small amount before bottling, or none at all), letting the wine develop naturally and accepting its instability and diversity; critics argue that without SO₂ protection the wine easily oxidises and develops faults (such as Brett and volatile acidity).
quiz.22.question: A sommelier opens a 2010 Barolo Riserva in a restaurant. What is the right way to decant it?
quiz.22.options.0: Pour straight into glasses; no decanting at all
quiz.22.options.1: Stand it upright before opening and decant slowly to remove the sediment; taste first to judge its state, and if still closed, aerate moderately for 1-2 hours
quiz.22.options.2: Put the whole bottle in 60°C hot water to speed up aeration
quiz.22.options.3: Don't decant at all — pour it straight into glasses, sediment and all, and drink at once
quiz.22.explanation: A 2010 Barolo Riserva has aged more than 15 years and will have sediment, but Nebbiolo's structure is still fairly youthful. Stand it upright before opening, decant slowly in front of a light to remove the sediment, and taste first: if still closed, aerate for another 1-2 hours. Vintages over 30 years old should be enjoyed straight after decanting, as long aeration may hasten their collapse.
quiz.23.question: In restaurant wine-list design, what is the most important criterion for choosing wines by the glass?
quiz.23.options.0: Choosing the most expensive wines to raise profit
quiz.23.options.1: Choosing wines that keep their quality for several days after opening and suit many dishes
quiz.23.options.2: Only local wines, avoiding international grapes
quiz.23.options.3: Only sweet wines, since most guests accept them
quiz.23.explanation: The core criteria for wines by the glass: stability after opening (high-acid whites such as Vermentino and Pinot Grigio keep better than low-acid wines; medium-tannin reds such as Barbera and Valpolicella are more stable than high-tannin aged wines), breadth of food pairing (versatile wines that suit starters through to mains), and reliability of supply (not a one-off small lot).
quiz.24.question: What is the correct serving temperature when a sommelier serves Italian Franciacorta DOCG sparkling wine?
quiz.24.options.0: At room temperature (18-20°C), letting the bubbles blend naturally
quiz.24.options.1: Chilled to 6-8°C, preserving fine bubbles and fresh acidity
quiz.24.options.2: With ice cubes to dilute it, for summer drinking
quiz.24.options.3: Warmed to 15°C first then gradually cooled, imitating Champagne
quiz.24.explanation: Like Champagne, Franciacorta is best served at 6-8°C. Low temperatures preserve fine bubbles (CO₂ is more soluble when cold), highlight fresh acidity and let the aromas of lees ageing (butter, biscuit) show more elegantly. An ice bucket (ice and water) cools more evenly than the fridge.
quiz.25.question: When pairing high-tannin reds (such as Barolo and Amarone) with food, which statement is most accurate?
quiz.25.options.0: High-tannin reds go with all seafood, as acidity balances fishiness
quiz.25.options.1: High-tannin reds go best with fatty red meat (fat softens tannin) and clash with delicate fish
quiz.25.options.2: High-tannin reds are ideal with dessert
quiz.25.options.3: High-tannin reds suit only cheese, not any dish
quiz.25.explanation: The pairing logic for high-tannin reds: fat coats the tannins and softens their astringency, so fatty red meats (steak, grilled lamb, braised beef) are the best match; with delicate seafood (raw fish, clams), the tannins are emphasised and taste harsher, and the seafood can take on a metallic, fishy note — a classic "clash".
quiz.26.question: What is the traditional winemaking and ageing character of Italian Vin Santo?
quiz.26.options.0: Made from Moscato and quickly fermented in stainless steel to keep fresh fruit
quiz.26.options.1: Made from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia and aged 3-10 years in small wooden casks (caratelli), developing oxidative complexity
quiz.26.options.2: Fortified with spirit to raise alcohol, like Marsala
quiz.26.options.3: Bled every autumn and bottled only after 25 years
quiz.26.explanation: Vin Santo is Tuscany's traditional sweet white: dried Trebbiano and Malvasia grapes, aged 3-10 years in small wooden caratelli (50-200 litres), developing oxidative aromas of nuts, caramel and beeswax. It is the traditional partner for cantucci (Italian almond biscuits) and is a semi-oxidative, long-aged style.
quiz.27.question: What is the definition of grappa, the Italian grape spirit?
quiz.27.options.0: A brandy distilled from any Italian wine
quiz.27.options.1: An Italian spirit distilled from pomace (vinacce: the skins, stems and seeds left after pressing)
quiz.27.options.2: A sweet fortified wine made from Muscat grapes
quiz.27.options.3: A traditional farm spirit distilled from olive pomace
quiz.27.explanation: Grappa is a legally protected Italian geographical-indication spirit: it must be distilled from Italian grape pomace (vinacce: the skins, stems and seeds after pressing), at 37.5-60% alcohol, and can only be produced in Italy. Single-variety (monovitigno) grappas such as Grappa di Moscato and Grappa di Nebbiolo are the highest-quality category.
quiz.28.question: What is the significance of Vermouth di Torino in Italy?
quiz.28.options.0: A Piemontese after-dinner dessert wine with no herbs
quiz.28.options.1: An aromatised, fortified aperitif made from a white-wine base infused with wormwood and other herbs, which must be produced in Piemonte; Torino is the birthplace of modern vermouth
quiz.28.options.2: A dry, sherry-style wine from Tuscany
quiz.28.options.3: A seasonal wine made only at Christmas
quiz.28.explanation: Vermouth di Torino IGP uses an Italian white-wine base infused with wormwood (the name comes from the German Wermut, meaning wormwood) and many herbs and spices, then fortified; it must be produced in Piemonte and comes in types such as Rosso, Bianco, Ambrato and Extra Dry. Torino is the 18th-century birthplace of modern vermouth (Carpano, 1786) and the home of Martini & Rossi and Cinzano.
quiz.29.question: What was the core contribution of the late Stanko Radikon (Friuli), a pioneer of Italian natural wine, to the orange-wine style?
quiz.29.options.0: Pioneering cool fermentation in stainless steel to keep whites fresh
quiz.29.options.1: Practising very long skin contact (months) + ageing in large oak casks (3-6 years) in Oslavia alongside Gravner, establishing Friuli's "epic" orange-wine style
quiz.29.options.2: Founding the first organic vineyard certification body
quiz.29.options.3: Inventing a modern technique of protecting orange wine from oxidation with carbon dioxide
quiz.29.explanation: Stanko Radikon (Radikon estate) and Josko Gravner are the twin giants of orange wine in Oslavia (on the Friuli-Collio border). Radikon's very long skin contact (fermenting Ribolla Gialla on its skins for 3-6 months) plus 3-6 years in large oak casks produced the most powerful orange wines, needing the most time to open — one of the holy grails for natural-wine collectors worldwide.
quiz.30.question: In Italian wine investment, which wines have the most liquid secondary market?
quiz.30.options.0: Everyday southern IGT reds, because of high volume and low prices
quiz.30.options.1: Barolo Riserva (top estates), Brunello di Montalcino, Super Tuscans (Sassicaia, Ornellaia, Masseto)
quiz.30.options.2: Prosecco DOCG, because sparkling wine is the most popular
quiz.30.options.3: Soave and Verdicchio, because white-wine ageing potential is most underrated
quiz.30.explanation: The most liquid Italian wines at auction are: Barolo (especially Giacomo Conterno Monfortino, Bartolo Mascarello, G.B. Burlotto), Brunello (Biondi-Santi, Soldera) and the Super Tuscans (Sassicaia, Ornellaia, Masseto). These wines have active secondary markets and clear price curves on platforms such as Wine-Searcher and Liv-ex.
quiz.31.question: Which statement best describes the difference between Oslavia's long-macerated orange wines and traditional Ramato?
quiz.31.options.0: The two are made the same way and are identical in style; only the name differs
quiz.31.options.1: Ramato: brief skin contact (1-3 days) for Pinot Grigio, a coppery-pink colour, fresh and easy; Friuli orange wines (Gravner/Radikon etc.): long skin contact (months), deep amber, high tannin, oxidative complexity
quiz.31.options.2: Ramato may only be produced in Friuli; it is a protected geographical indication
quiz.31.options.3: Friuli orange wine must use amphorae, and Ramato must use oak
quiz.31.explanation: Ramato (Italian for "coppery") is the traditional Veneto/Friuli method for Pinot Grigio with brief skin contact (1-3 days), giving a coppery-pink colour and a fresh style with no need for ageing; Oslavia-style orange wines (Gravner, Radikon) are macerated for months and aged for years in large oak or amphorae, deep amber, high in tannin and strongly oxidative — a completely different stylistic category.
quiz.32.question: What problem with Italy's DOC system did the birth of the "Super Tuscans" in the 1970s-80s reveal?
quiz.32.options.0: DOC rules were so strict that even the finest traditional wines could not pass
quiz.32.options.1: DOC rules were outdated (such as compulsory white grapes and limits on international varieties), so top winemakers innovated instead as Vino da Tavola (IGT after 1992)
quiz.32.options.2: The government required all fine wines to be exported, so they could not be sold in Italy
quiz.32.options.3: The DOC system did not yet exist in the 1970s; Super Tuscans were born in a legal vacuum
quiz.32.explanation: The Super Tuscans had two motives: 1) escaping restrictions (DOC rules at the time often reflected outdated standards, such as Chianti requiring white grapes); 2) active innovation (in the 1970s Antinori's Tignanello dropped the white grapes, added Cabernet and voluntarily became a Vino da Tavola). This showed how conservative the DOC system was then: quality innovation was forced "outside the law" until the IGT category was created in 1992.
quiz.33.question: In current Italian wine law, what does "Classico" mean (as in Chianti Classico, Soave Classico)?
quiz.33.options.0: Made by the "traditional method" without any modern equipment
quiz.33.options.1: The historic core zone (the original growing area, older and better situated than the outer zones)
quiz.33.options.2: Aged at least 10 years and suited to long cellaring
quiz.33.options.3: Made only from organically farmed vineyards
quiz.33.explanation: "Classico" in Italian law means the historic core zone, i.e. the original growing area before the denomination was enlarged. Chianti Classico (core villages such as Greve, Gaiole and Castelnuovo Berardenga), for example, was established earlier than the outer Chianti zones and generally has better soils and climate, so it keeps its own Classico framework.
quiz.34.question: What was the impact of the 2008 "Brunello Gate" scandal on the Italian wine industry?
quiz.34.options.0: It almost destroyed Brunello's international reputation, which has still not recovered
quiz.34.options.1: It led the DOCG to strengthen variety traceability and testing, reinforcing Italy's quality-control system in the long term
quiz.34.options.2: The US market banned all Italian wine imports for 5 years
quiz.34.options.3: It affected only the 3 estates involved in adulteration, with no impact on the market
quiz.34.explanation: In 2008 "Brunello Gate" (Brunellopoli) broke out when prosecutors' investigations found that some estates were suspected of blending other grapes into Brunello (against the 100% Sangiovese rule). The scandal shook the market in the short term, but in the long term it led the area to strengthen vineyard registration, traceability of origin and testing, actually reinforcing Brunello's credibility — a classic case of "crisis into opportunity".
quiz.35.question: In the Level 3 course, which description of the conservation value of "rare grapes" is most profound?
quiz.35.options.0: Rare grapes are just a marketing gimmick and cannot compete on quality with mainstream grapes
quiz.35.options.1: Rare grapes are a gene bank of thousands of years of Italian farming culture, providing diversity and resilience against climate change, and are key to differentiated market positioning
quiz.35.options.2: All rare grapes should be replanted with modern high-yielding varieties to raise Italy's total output
quiz.35.options.3: Conserving rare grapes is purely academic, with no commercial meaning for the wine industry
quiz.35.explanation: Rare-grape conservation has several meanings: 1) cultural heritage (each grape is the product of centuries of human selection and farming wisdom); 2) climate resilience (native grapes are often better adapted to local conditions than imported commercial varieties, as with Timorasso and Nosiola); 3) market differentiation (rarity itself creates a premium position, as with the recent international attention on Ruché).
quiz.36.question: After completing Level 3, what is the correct description of Italian wine's position in the global fine-wine market?
quiz.36.options.0: Italian wine is forever just a second-rate substitute for French wine
quiz.36.options.1: Through the diversity of its native grapes, the expressiveness of its regions and its long farming culture, Italian wine has established an irreplaceable, unique position in the global fine-wine market
quiz.36.options.2: Italian wine's greatest strength is low prices and mass production
quiz.36.options.3: Italian wine is far ahead of France in Asia and the main source of high-end wine there
quiz.36.explanation: The core of Italy's position in the global fine-wine market: more than 350 native grapes (unmatched diversity), the distinctive terroirs of 20 regions, 3,000 years of wine-growing culture and a quality revolution over the last 30 years have given Italian wine an irreplaceable position alongside France and Spain, built on "historical depth × breadth of grapes × regional precision".
quiz.37.question: Regarding Italian wine service, which sommelier behaviour is most professional?
quiz.37.options.0: Pouring every type of wine into a standard ISO tasting glass to save time
quiz.37.options.1: Choosing different glasses by wine type (a large Nebbiolo bowl for Barolo, a Burgundy glass for Brunello, a slender flute for sparkling wine) and briefly introducing the wine's background before serving
quiz.37.options.2: Decanting every Italian wine 5 hours in advance, regardless of vintage or style
quiz.37.options.3: Always recommending only the most expensive wines to boost sales
quiz.37.explanation: The core of professional wine service is "glass choice × decanting judgement × guest communication": wide-bowled glasses (Burgundy / Nebbiolo type) suit Barolo and Barbaresco, which need air to open; flutes keep bubbles; decanting time must be judged by the wine's vintage and style (not one size fits all); introducing the wine's background helps guests appreciate it and builds trust.

slides.1.title: 📚 Scope and Instructions
slides.1.content:
This assessment covers expert-level knowledge from the whole Level 3 course, with 38 questions.

🍇 Rare grapes: Timorasso, Ruché, Erbaluce, Nosiola and the orange-wine revolution
🗺️ Classification in depth: the MGA system, the fascetta, the legal meaning of Riserva and Classico
📅 Vintage assessment: climate factors, top Barolo/Brunello vintages
👁️ Blind-tasting technique: the SAT method, grape identifiers, style comparisons
🏭 The industry in depth: the investment market, natural wine, climate warming, regulatory change
🍽️ Service in practice: decanting, pairing principles, glass choice, restaurant strategy

Suggested time: 60 minutes | Pass mark: 70 (at least 27 correct)
slides.2.title: 🎯 Level 3 Key Points
slides.2.points.0: 🍇 Rare white grape: Timorasso (Piemonte, revived by Walter Massa) → "Italy's Riesling"
slides.2.points.1: 🌹 Rare red grape: Ruché (Castagnole Monferrato DOCG, rose-petal aromas)
slides.2.points.2: 🌄 Erbaluce di Caluso DOCG: the Canavese in Piemonte, with its rare sweet Passito
slides.2.points.3: 🍯 Nosiola: the Valle dei Laghi in Trentino, Vino Santo — a sweet white dried until Holy Week and aged for years
slides.2.points.4: 🍊 Orange-wine pioneer: Josko Gravner (Oslavia) revived the ancient method of skin maceration in clay vessels in the late 1990s
slides.2.points.5: 🧡 Stanko Radikon: the other great master of Oslavia orange wine, Ribolla Gialla macerated for months and aged for years
slides.2.points.6: 🗺️ MGA (Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive): the vineyard geographical-mention system of Barbaresco (2007) and Barolo (2010), not a quality ranking
slides.2.points.7: 🌍 Barolo's geological divide: Serralunga (Serravallian calcareous marl and sandstone, powerful) vs La Morra (Tortonian calcareous marl, aromatic)
slides.2.points.8: 🔒 Fascetta: the uniquely numbered state guarantee seal of DOCG, traceable by serial number
slides.2.points.9: 📜 Riserva: a longer legal ageing period than the normal wine (rules vary by DOC)
slides.2.points.11: 📅 Legendary Brunello vintage: 1997 (officially five stars, enthusiastically praised internationally)
slides.2.points.12: 🏠 Cellar conditions: 12-14°C, 70-75% humidity, dark and still, corked bottles lying down
slides.2.points.13: 👁️ SAT blind tasting: sight (appearance) → aroma (still, then swirled) → taste (attack, mid-palate, finish)
slides.2.points.14: 🎯 Nebbiolo identifiers: garnet + orange rim + tar/rose/dried leaves + high acid and high tannin
slides.2.points.15: ⚗️ Biodynamic preparation 500: cow manure in a horn fermented over winter, diluted, stirred and sprayed on the land
slides.2.points.16: 🌡️ Warming: short-term gains for high-altitude northern Italy; long-term water and acidity crises in the South
slides.2.points.17: 🍷 Natural wine: no or very little added SO₂, accepting the instability of natural evolution
slides.2.points.18: 🥃 Grappa: distilled from grape pomace (vinacce), a legally protected Italian GI spirit
slides.2.points.19: 🥂 Vermouth di Torino IGP: white wine + wormwood + herbs, made in Piemonte; Torino is the birthplace of modern vermouth
slides.2.points.20: 🍯 Vin Santo: dried Trebbiano/Malvasia + oxidative ageing for 3-10 years in small caratelli
slides.2.points.21: 💰 Investment stars: Barolo Riserva (Conterno Monfortino), Brunello Riserva (Biondi-Santi), the Super Tuscans
slides.2.points.22: 🏺 Ramato (coppery, brief skin contact) vs Oslavia's deep orange wines (long maceration, years of ageing): two completely different philosophies of orange wine
slides.2.points.23: ⚖️ The logic behind the Super Tuscans: outdated DOC rules → voluntary declassification to Vino da Tavola (IGT after 1992) to innovate
slides.2.points.24: 🔍 Brunello Gate (2008): short-term shock → long-term strengthening of traceability and controls
slides.2.points.25: 🎓 Congratulations on completing Level 3! You now have expert-level knowledge of Italian wine
